title: Daily revenue is triple what finance booked
ticket: Finance: the dashboard says yesterday made $36,000; Stripe payouts say $12,000. The numbers diverge more on days with big baskets.

lines: JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id

failing.test: daily_revenue: one paid order of $120 with three items

explanation.cause: Joining to order_items repeats each order once per item, so the order total is summed once per line.
explanation.why: Summing at the grain of the join, item price times quantity, counts each item once. Dividing by three only fixes this one order; the average trick still double counts, and MAX returns one order, not the day's total.

title: Late-evening events land in the wrong day's partition
ticket: Events from our New York customers after 7 pm keep showing up in the next day's table, and yesterday's totals change after midnight UTC.

lines: """The UTC day an event belongs to, as YYYY-MM-DD."""

explanation.cause: fromtimestamp without a tz converts to the server's local zone, so the date depends on where the job runs.
explanation.why: Asking for UTC explicitly makes the partition the event's UTC day everywhere. utcnow() ignores the event's own time entirely, and astimezone() still lands in the local zone.

title: Net revenue: subtract refunds
author: Omar Haddad
description: Finance wants net revenue, so this joins refunds and subtracts them from each order's total.

diff.text: JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.id

explanation.cause: An inner join keeps only orders that have a refund, so every order without one drops out of revenue.
explanation.why: It needs a LEFT JOIN with refunds pre-aggregated per order and COALESCE(..., 0); otherwise net revenue is a small fraction of the real figure, and an order refunded twice still double counts.

title: Index events by user and time for the activity page
author: Elena Ruiz
description: The activity page filters events by user and sorts by time, and it's a sequential scan over 900M rows. Adding the index concurrently so writes keep flowing.

diff.text: -- Runs outside a transaction: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can't run inside one.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS events_user_created_idx
-- If it fails, the index is left INVALID: drop it and run this again.

explanation.cause: Nothing wrong: the column order matches the query, and it's built concurrently.
explanation.why: user_id first serves the filter and created_at DESC serves the sort. It runs outside a transaction as CONCURRENTLY requires, and the comment covers the invalid-index case, which is exactly what bit the orders migration.
